lessons.title: Purity, formulations and chromatography
lessons.summary: Learn what a chemist means by 'pure', how melting points reveal impurities, why so many everyday products are carefully designed mixtures, and how paper chromatography separates and identifies substances.
objectives: I can explain what a pure substance is in chemistry and how this differs from everyday use of the word.
I can use melting and boiling point data to decide whether a substance is pure.
I can describe what a formulation is and give examples.
I can describe how paper chromatography separates a mixture and interpret a chromatogram.
I can calculate Rf values and use them to identify substances.

activities.title: What does 'pure' mean?
activities.content:
## Two meanings of one word

In everyday life, "pure orange juice" means juice with nothing added. To a chemist, orange juice is nowhere near pure: it is a mixture of water, sugars, acids, vitamins and dozens of other compounds.

In chemistry, a **pure substance** is a **single element or compound, not mixed with anything else**. Pure water contains only H₂O molecules. Pure gold contains only gold atoms.

### How to test for purity

Every pure substance has a **sharp, fixed melting point and boiling point**. Pure water boils at exactly 100 °C at atmospheric pressure and pure ice melts at exactly 0 °C.

A **mixture** behaves differently:

- It melts over a **range** of temperatures rather than at one fixed point.
- Impurities **lower the melting point** and **raise the boiling point**.

So if a sample of "pure" aspirin starts to melt at 128 °C and does not finish until 134 °C, it is impure. Pure aspirin melts sharply at 136 °C.

This is why salt is spread on icy roads: salt water freezes well below 0 °C, so the ice melts. And it is why adding salt to cooking water raises its boiling point slightly.

You can compare the measured melting point of a sample with the value in a data book to check its purity.

activities.title: Worked example: reading melting point data
activities.content:
**A student tests four white powders. Which are pure?**

| Sample | Melting starts | Melting finishes | Data book value |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 80 °C | 80 °C | 80 °C |
| B | 71 °C | 78 °C | 80 °C |
| C | 122 °C | 122 °C | 122 °C |
| D | 115 °C | 120 °C | 122 °C |

**A** melts sharply at exactly the data book value, so it is **pure**.

**B** melts over a 7 °C range and starts below the data book value, so it is an **impure** version of A.

**C** is **pure**: sharp melting point matching the data book.

**D** melts over a range and below the expected value, so it is **impure**.

**Two signs of impurity to quote in an exam:**
1. Melting occurs over a range of temperatures.
2. The melting point is lower than the expected value.

The more impurity there is, the wider the range and the lower the starting temperature.

question.text: A liquid is heated and starts to boil at 103 °C. The temperature keeps rising while it boils, reaching 107 °C. What can you conclude?
question.hint: Pure substances boil at one fixed temperature.
question.explanation: A pure substance boils at a single fixed temperature. Boiling over a range means the liquid is a mixture (impure).

options.text: The liquid is a mixture because it boils over a range of temperatures.
The liquid is pure because it boils above 100 °C.
options.feedback: Boiling above 100 °C does not prove purity; many pure liquids boil at other temperatures.
Pure water boils at exactly 100 °C and stays there.

activities.title: Formulations
activities.content:
## Mixtures designed on purpose

Most of the products in your bathroom, kitchen and garage are not pure substances. They are **formulations**.

A **formulation** is a **mixture that has been designed as a useful product**. Each component is added in a **carefully measured quantity** so that the product has exactly the properties needed.

### Examples

| Formulation | Some components | Why each is there |
|---|---|---|
| paint | pigment, solvent, binder | colour, spreads easily, sticks and dries hard |
| medicine tablet | active drug, filler, coating | correct dose, right size to handle, easy to swallow |
| fertiliser | nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds | balanced plant nutrients |
| alloy (e.g. steel) | iron, carbon, other metals | strength, hardness, corrosion resistance |
| fuel | hydrocarbons, additives | burns cleanly, protects the engine |
| cleaning product | detergent, water, fragrance | removes grease, pleasant smell |

### The key idea

A formulation is not a random mixture. Change the proportions and the product changes. A paint with too little binder flakes off; a tablet with the wrong amount of drug could be dangerous.

The word to use in exams: a formulation is **"a mixture with a specific purpose, in which each component is present in a fixed, measured amount"**.

question.text: Which of the following are formulations? Select all that apply.
question.hint: A formulation is a mixture made to a recipe for a purpose. A single compound is not a formulation.
question.explanation: Paint and a painkiller tablet are mixtures made to precise recipes. Distilled water and pure copper are single substances, so they are not formulations.

options.feedback: Distilled water is a pure compound, not a mixture.

activities.title: Paper chromatography
activities.content:
## Separating a mixture of dissolved substances

**Chromatography** separates the substances in a mixture and can help identify them. It is used in forensics, food testing and checking medicines.

### The method

1. Draw a **pencil** line about 1 cm from the bottom of a strip of chromatography paper. Pencil is used because graphite does not dissolve and move; ink would.
2. Put a small **spot** of the mixture on the line. Keep it small so the separated spots do not overlap.
3. Stand the paper in a beaker with a shallow layer of **solvent** (water or ethanol). The solvent level must be **below** the line, or the sample would wash off into the beaker.
4. Cover the beaker with a lid so the solvent does not evaporate.
5. Let the solvent rise up the paper. Take the paper out before the solvent reaches the top and mark the **solvent front** with pencil.

### The two phases

- The **stationary phase** is the paper. It does not move.
- The **mobile phase** is the solvent. It moves up the paper carrying the substances with it.

### Why substances separate

Each substance is pulled two ways: it is **attracted to the paper** and it is **dissolved by the solvent**. A substance that dissolves well in the solvent and is only weakly attracted to the paper travels **far**. One that is strongly attracted to the paper travels only a **short way**. Different substances strike a different balance, so they end up at different heights.

The finished paper, with its pattern of spots, is called a **chromatogram**.

activities.title: Worked example: reading a chromatogram
activities.content:
**A black ink is run alongside four known dyes. The chromatogram shows:**

```
 solvent front ------------------------

   ink    red   blue   green  yellow
    o                            o      <- high
    o            o                      <- middle
    o     o                             <- low
  ---------------------------------- start line
```

**Which dyes are in the ink?**

The ink separated into **three spots**, so it contains **at least three** substances (it is a mixture).

Compare the heights:
- The ink's low spot is level with **red**.
- Its middle spot is level with **blue**.
- Its high spot is level with **yellow**.

Spots at the **same height** in the **same solvent** are very likely the **same substance**. So the ink contains red, blue and yellow dyes. Green has no matching spot, so it is not present.

**What if a substance gave only one spot in every solvent tested?**

That suggests it is a **pure** substance. A pure substance always gives a single spot. (One spot in a single solvent is weaker evidence, since two substances might happen to travel the same distance in that solvent.)

question.text: Put the steps of paper chromatography in the correct order.
question.hint: The start line must be drawn before the spot is added, and the solvent goes in last before running.
question.explanation: Draw the pencil line, add the spot, place the paper in the solvent with the level below the line, let the solvent rise, then mark the solvent front.
order: Draw a pencil line near the bottom of the paper
Put a small spot of the mixture on the line
Stand the paper in solvent with the level below the line
Allow the solvent to rise up the paper
Remove the paper and mark the solvent front

activities.title: Rf values
activities.content:
## Putting a number on each spot

How far a spot travels depends on how far the solvent travelled, so different runs cannot be compared directly. Instead we use the **Rf value** (retention factor):

$R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the substance}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent}}$

Both distances are measured **from the start line**: to the **centre** of the spot for the substance, and to the **solvent front** for the solvent.

### What the number tells you

- Rf is always **between 0 and 1** (the spot cannot overtake the solvent).
- Rf has **no units**, because it is one distance divided by another.
- A **high** Rf (near 1) means the substance is very soluble in the solvent and travels almost with the solvent front.
- A **low** Rf (near 0) means it is strongly attracted to the paper.

### Identifying substances

For a given substance in a given solvent at a given temperature, the Rf value is **always the same**. So you can measure the Rf of an unknown spot and compare it with a table of known values.

Change the solvent and the Rf values change, because the balance between paper and solvent is different. That is why a solvent must always be stated alongside an Rf value.

activities.title: Worked example: calculating and using Rf
activities.content:
**On a chromatogram the solvent front is 8.0 cm from the start line. Spot X is 6.0 cm from the start line and spot Y is 2.0 cm. Calculate their Rf values.**

$R_f(X) = \dfrac{6.0}{8.0} = 0.75$

$R_f(Y) = \dfrac{2.0}{8.0} = 0.25$

**A data table for the same solvent gives these values:**

| Substance | Rf |
|---|---|
| tartrazine | 0.25 |
| sunset yellow | 0.50 |
| carmoisine | 0.75 |

X matches **carmoisine** and Y matches **tartrazine**.

**The reverse calculation.** If a substance has Rf = 0.4 and the solvent front travels 12.5 cm, how far does the spot move?

distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.4 × 12.5 = **5.0 cm**

**Measuring tip:** always measure to the middle of the spot, and use the same ruler and the same zero for both distances.

question.text: On a chromatogram the solvent front moved 9.6 cm from the start line and a spot moved 7.2 cm. Calculate the Rf value of the spot.
question.hint: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent.

metadata.blanksText: In paper chromatography the paper is the ___ phase and the solvent is the ___ phase. A substance that is more soluble in the solvent travels ___ up the paper.

question.hint: One phase moves and one stays still. More soluble substances go with the solvent.
question.explanation: The paper is the stationary phase; the solvent is the mobile phase; more soluble substances travel further.

question.text:
A food scientist uses paper chromatography to find out whether a sweet contains the banned dye E123. She runs a spot of colouring from the sweet next to a spot of pure E123 in the same solvent.

(a) Explain why the start line is drawn in pencil, not ink.

(b) Explain why the solvent level must be below the start line.

(c) The colouring from the sweet separates into three spots. The pure E123 gives one spot. State what this shows about the two samples.

(d) The E123 spot moves 4.5 cm and the solvent front moves 7.5 cm. Calculate the Rf value of E123. One of the spots from the sweet has an Rf value of 0.60. What does the scientist conclude?
question.hint: Ink would dissolve. The spot would wash away. Count the spots. Compare the Rf values.
question.explanation: (a) Ink would dissolve in the solvent and move up the paper, adding extra spots. (b) If the solvent covered the start line, the spots would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker instead of moving up the paper. (c) The sweet colouring is a mixture of at least three substances; E123 is a pure substance. (d) Rf = 4.5 ÷ 7.5 = 0.60. The sweet's spot has the same Rf as E123 in the same solvent, so the sweet does contain E123.

markScheme.criterion: Ink would dissolve in the solvent and move / separate, confusing the results
The sample would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker / wash off the paper
The sweet colouring is a mixture (of at least three substances) and E123 is pure
Same Rf value in the same solvent, so the sweet contains E123

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- In chemistry, a **pure substance** is a single element or compound. Everyday "pure" just means nothing added.
- Pure substances have **sharp, fixed** melting and boiling points. Impurities **lower** the melting point, **raise** the boiling point, and make melting happen over a **range**.
- A **formulation** is a mixture designed for a purpose, with each component in a **measured amount**: paints, medicines, alloys, fuels, fertilisers, cleaning products.
- **Paper chromatography**: pencil line, small spot, solvent below the line, lid on. Paper = **stationary phase**, solvent = **mobile phase**.
- Substances separate because they differ in how strongly they are attracted to the paper versus dissolved by the solvent.
- **Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent**. No units, 0 to 1, fixed for a substance in a given solvent. Same Rf as a known substance suggests the same identity.
- A pure substance gives **one spot**; a mixture gives **several**.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: in chemistry, milk is a pure substance.
practiceQuestions.hint: Milk contains water, fats, proteins and sugars.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Milk is a mixture of many compounds, so it is not chemically pure, even if nothing has been added to it.

practiceQuestions.text: What is the mobile phase in paper chromatography?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The solvent moves up the paper, carrying the dissolved substances, so it is the mobile phase. The paper is the stationary phase.

options.feedback: The paper stays still, so it is the stationary phase.

metadata.blanksText: Adding an impurity to a pure solid ___ its melting point, and adding an impurity to a pure liquid ___ its boiling point.

practiceQuestions.hint: Salt on icy roads; salt in cooking water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point.

practiceQuestions.text: A spot moves 3.0 cm and the solvent front moves 12.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value.
practiceQuestions.hint: Divide the smaller distance by the larger.

practiceQuestions.text: A substance has an Rf value of 0.35 in ethanol. If the solvent front travels 14.0 cm, how far in cm will the spot travel?
practiceQuestions.hint: Rearrange: distance of spot = Rf × distance of solvent.

practiceQuestions.text: Two substances have Rf values of 0.9 and 0.2 in the same solvent. Which statement is correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: A high Rf means the substance travels almost as far as the solvent.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A high Rf means the substance is more soluble in the solvent (or less attracted to the paper), so it travels further. Rf values have no units and cannot exceed 1.

options.text: The substance with Rf 0.9 is more soluble in the solvent than the one with Rf 0.2.
The substance with Rf 0.2 travelled further up the paper.
The Rf values are measured in centimetres.
options.feedback: Rf is a ratio and has no units.

options.text: The substance with Rf 0.9 must be a mixture.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each formulation to a reason one of its components is included.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what each product needs to do.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Paint needs a pigment for colour; a tablet needs a filler so the tiny dose of drug makes a tablet big enough to handle; a fertiliser needs nitrogen compounds because plants need nitrogen to grow.

pairs.right: filler to make the tablet a usable size

practiceQuestions.text: A student obtains a single spot when running a sample in water. Which of these statements are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: One spot in one solvent is suggestive but not proof.
practiceQuestions.explanation: One spot is consistent with a pure substance, but two substances could happen to have the same Rf in water, so running the sample in a second solvent is a sensible check. It does not prove the sample is a mixture.

options.text: The sample may be a pure substance.
Running the sample in a different solvent would be a useful check.
The sample is definitely a mixture.
The sample cannot contain any coloured substance.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why different substances in a mixture separate during paper chromatography.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the two things acting on each substance: the paper and the solvent.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each substance has a different balance between its attraction to the paper (stationary phase) and its solubility in the solvent (mobile phase). Substances that are more soluble or less attracted to the paper move further, so the spots end up at different heights.

markScheme.criterion: Substances differ in solubility in the solvent / attraction to the paper
So they move different distances / at different speeds up the paper

practiceQuestions.text:
A pharmacist has a batch of paracetamol tablets and wants to check that the paracetamol in them is pure. Pure paracetamol melts at 169 °C.

(a) Describe how the pharmacist could use melting point to check the purity, and state what result would show the sample is pure.

(b) Explain why the tablet itself would not give a sharp melting point even if the paracetamol inside it is pure.

(c) Suggest one other method the pharmacist could use to check purity, and say what result would be expected for a pure sample.
practiceQuestions.hint: Heat a small sample slowly and watch the temperature. A tablet is a formulation. Chromatography gives a characteristic result for pure substances.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Heat a small sample of the extracted paracetamol slowly in a melting point apparatus and record the temperature at which it melts; a pure sample melts sharply at 169 °C. (b) A tablet is a formulation containing fillers, binders and coatings as well as paracetamol, so it is a mixture and melts over a range. (c) Chromatography: a pure sample gives a single spot (with the Rf value expected for paracetamol).

markScheme.criterion: Heat a sample and measure the temperature at which it melts (compare with data)
Pure sample melts sharply at 169 °C; impure would melt over a range / below 169 °C
The tablet is a formulation / mixture containing other substances (fillers, binders), so it melts over a range
Chromatography: a pure sample gives one spot

practiceQuestions.text: A white solid is heated slowly. It begins to melt at 52 °C and has completely melted by 58 °C. What can you conclude?
practiceQuestions.hint: A pure substance melts at one sharp temperature.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A pure substance melts completely at a single fixed temperature. Melting over a range of temperatures shows that the solid contains more than one substance, so it is a mixture (impure).

options.text: The solid is a mixture because it melts over a range of temperatures.
The solid is pure because it melts below 100 °C.
options.feedback: The value of the melting point does not tell you about purity; the sharpness does.

options.text: The solid is pure because it has a low melting point.

practiceQuestions.text: A student sorts some everyday materials into formulations and non-formulations. Which of these should go in the formulations group? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: A formulation is a useful mixture in which each component is added in a measured amount for a purpose.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Toothpaste and a garden fertiliser are mixtures blended to a recipe so that each ingredient does a job. A bar of pure gold is a single element and pure sodium chloride is a single compound, so neither is a formulation.

options.feedback: Pure gold is a single element, not a mixture.
A single compound is not a formulation.

practiceQuestions.text: A student has run a paper chromatogram. Put the steps in order to find the Rf value of one of the spots.
practiceQuestions.hint: The solvent front must be marked as soon as the paper comes out, before anything is measured.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Stop the run when the solvent is near the top, mark the solvent front straight away (it will dry and become invisible), measure the distance to the spot and to the solvent front from the start line, then divide the spot distance by the solvent distance.
order: Remove the paper when the solvent is near the top
Mark the position of the solvent front in pencil
Measure the distance from the start line to the centre of the spot
Measure the distance from the start line to the solvent front
Divide the spot distance by the solvent distance

practiceQuestions.text: A dye is run on a chromatogram. The solvent front travels 13.5 cm from the start line and the dye spot travels 5.4 cm. Calculate the Rf value of the dye.
practiceQuestions.hint: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front. Rf has no units.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about how substances behave in chromatography.

metadata.blanksText: In chromatography the solvent that moves through the paper is the ___ phase. A substance that is more soluble in the solvent travels further, so it has a ___ Rf value (higher or lower). A pure substance always produces ___ spot on the chromatogram.

practiceQuestions.hint: One phase moves and one stays still. Rf compares the spot distance with the solvent distance. Think about how many substances a pure sample contains.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The solvent is the mobile phase. More soluble substances are carried further, giving a higher Rf value. A pure substance contains only one compound, so it gives only one spot.

practiceQuestions.text:
A forensic scientist uses paper chromatography to find out which of two pens, A or B, was used to write a note. She runs a spot of ink from the note next to spots of ink from each pen, all in the same solvent.

(a) Explain why all three samples must be run in the same solvent.

(b) The ink from the note separates into two spots. Pen A gives one spot and pen B gives two spots. State what the results show about the ink from the note.

(c) The two spots from pen B move 3.6 cm and 6.0 cm; the solvent front moves 8.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value of each spot from pen B. The spots from the note have Rf values of 0.45 and 0.75. What does the scientist conclude?

(d) Explain why the scientist marks the solvent front in pencil as soon as the paper is removed from the solvent.
practiceQuestions.hint: Rf depends on the solvent. Count the spots. Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance. Think about what happens to a wet solvent front as the paper dries.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The Rf value of a substance depends on the solvent used, so the samples can only be compared fairly if the same solvent is used. (b) The ink from the note is a mixture of at least two substances. (c) Rf = 3.6 ÷ 8.0 = 0.45 and 6.0 ÷ 8.0 = 0.75. These match the Rf values of the note's spots in the same solvent, so pen B was used. (d) The solvent evaporates as the paper dries, so the position of the solvent front would no longer be visible and the Rf values could not be calculated.

markScheme.criterion: Rf values depend on the solvent, so the same solvent is needed for a fair comparison
The ink from the note is a mixture (of at least two substances)
Same Rf values as the note, so pen B was used
The solvent evaporates / dries so the front would no longer be visible
